reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Eosinophilic infiltration of the small bowel, part of the eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders and frequently overlapping with gastric involvement as eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

The Klein depth classification applies: mucosal disease causes malabsorption, diarrhoea, protein-losing enteropathy and iron deficiency; muscular disease causes obstruction; serosal disease causes eosinophilic ascites.
Malabsorption and weight loss are prominent with mucosal involvement.
Peripheral eosinophilia is common and atopy is frequent.
Diagnosis rests on small-bowel biopsies (which may need enteroscopy or capsule endoscopy) showing excess eosinophils after excluding secondary causes.
Parasitic infection such as Strongyloides, Anisakis or hookworm is a key mimic and must be excluded.
Corticosteroids are the mainstay, with dietary elimination in selected cases.
Patchy, deep or transmural disease may be missed on standard mucosal biopsy.
reference.pathophysiology: Eosinophilic enteritis reflects antigen-driven Th2 inflammation of the small intestine, with interleukin-5 and interleukin-13-mediated recruitment of eosinophils whose degranulation injures the mucosa and deeper layers. Mucosal infiltration disrupts the absorptive surface and enteric barrier, causing malabsorption and protein loss; muscular involvement thickens and stiffens the bowel wall producing subacute obstruction; and serosal involvement generates eosinophil-rich ascites. Food allergens and an atopic diathesis are frequently implicated.
additionalInvestigations: Device-assisted enteroscopy or capsule endoscopy with small-bowel biopsies
Full blood count with eosinophil count
Coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA) with total IgA
Serum albumin and markers of protein-losing enteropathy
CT or MR enterography for wall thickening, obstruction or ascites
ANCA and connective tissue screen where vasculitis is suspected
redFlags: Severe malabsorption with weight loss and hypoalbuminaemia
Features suggesting lymphoma or systemic vasculitis
reference.prognosis: Eosinophilic enteritis often responds well to corticosteroids with symptomatic and histological improvement, but relapse is common and some patients require long-term immunomodulation or dietary therapy.
pitfalls: Missing patchy or deep (muscular or serosal) disease with superficial biopsies alone
Failing to exclude Strongyloides before immunosuppression
Confusing the picture with coeliac disease or Crohn's disease
Attributing the eosinophilia to the bowel while overlooking systemic hypereosinophilic syndrome
